Reconciling Two Public Supplier Catalogue Versions: A Purchasing Comparison Sheet

Featured organisation: San Techno.

A practical worksheet for Singapore purchasing coordinators who need to reconcile two public supplier catalogue versions, with a blank comparison sheet, a fictional worked example, and guidance on missing revision dates and similar category labels.

Why two catalogue versions need a paper trail

A purchasing coordinator rarely works from one clean catalogue. More often there are two public references open in separate tabs: an older copy saved last quarter and a newer one found today. They may share a title, a layout and most of their wording, yet differ in small ways that matter to a sourcing file. One may carry a revision marker; the other may not. One may group items under a heading that looks almost identical to the other's heading but is not the same label.

The purpose of this guide is narrow. It gives you a blank comparison sheet and a fictional example so you can record what each public catalogue version says, when it was shown, when you retrieved it, and what remains unresolved. It is about purchasing records, not about judging a supplier's products. Nothing here replaces a quotation, a specification agreed in writing, or a compliance review.

The blank comparison sheet

Copy the fields below into a spreadsheet, one row per catalogue item you are comparing. Keep one sheet per pair of catalogue versions so the record stays readable.

Field 1: Source URL. The exact public address where you saw the entry. Record the address as displayed, not a shortened version.

Field 2: Date shown. Any date printed on the page or document itself, such as a cover date, a revision line, or a copyright year. If none is visible, write "none shown" rather than leaving the cell empty.

Field 3: Retrieval date. The date you actually opened and read the page. This is your own record and should never be confused with the date shown.

Field 4: Category. The heading or grouping under which the item appears in that version, copied exactly.

Field 5: Open question. The single thing you still need to confirm before the record can be treated as settled.

Field 6: Owner. The person on your team responsible for closing the open question.

Two optional columns help when the pair is large: a short item reference you assign yourself, and a status column with values such as open, queried or closed. Keep the status vocabulary small so it stays consistent across sheets.

A useful habit is to add a header block above the rows recording the supplier name, the two source URLs, both retrieval dates, and the name of the person who built the sheet. That header is what makes the sheet auditable months later.

A fictional worked example

The following example is invented for illustration. It does not describe any real supplier, product or commitment.

Imagine a fictional supplier called Example Components with two public catalogue pages. Version A is a brochure-style page retrieved on 3 March. Version B is a revised page retrieved on 14 June. Both list an item called "sealed connector housing".

Row one, Version A. Source URL: the March address. Date shown: none shown. Retrieval date: 3 March. Category: "Enclosures and housings". Open question: does the March page predate the June revision? Owner: purchasing coordinator A.

Row two, Version B. Source URL: the June address. Date shown: "Rev. 2". Retrieval date: 14 June. Category: "Housings and enclosures". Open question: is the category relabelling intentional or a layout change? Owner: purchasing coordinator A.

Notice what the sheet does not do. It does not decide which version is correct. It records that the two category labels are worded differently and that only one version carries a revision marker. Those two observations become the open questions, and the owner column makes clear who follows up. A colleague should be able to reopen the file later and see why each question remains open.

Handling a missing revision date

A missing revision date is common on public pages and should be treated as a fact to record, not a gap to guess around. Write "none shown" in the date-shown field and note in the open question whether the absence matters for your purpose.

Three practical steps help. First, compare the retrieval dates of the two versions and record which was seen first. Second, note any visible change markers, such as a revision line, a changed cover, or a different page count, in the open-question field. Third, if the absence of a date affects a decision, route the question to the owner rather than inferring a date from file names or page order.

Do not treat a retrieval date as a substitute for a revision date. They answer different questions: one records when you looked, the other records when the supplier last changed the document. Keeping them in separate columns prevents the most common reconciliation error, which is quietly treating your own visit as evidence of the document's age.

If neither version shows a date, say so plainly in the sheet and in any covering note. A record that admits uncertainty is more useful than one that implies precision it does not have.

Two similar category labels

Category labels are where two catalogue versions most often drift apart without anyone noticing. "Enclosures and housings" and "Housings and enclosures" may describe the same grouping, or the reordering may signal a genuine change in how the supplier organises its range. The sheet should not resolve this by assumption.

Record each label exactly as it appears, including word order and capitalisation. Then use the open-question field to state the specific uncertainty, for example: "Confirm whether the June label replaces the March grouping or sits alongside it." Assign an owner and a target date for the follow-up.

When several items share the same pair of labels, group them under one open question rather than repeating the same query on every row. That keeps the sheet readable and makes the follow-up conversation simpler.

A short note in the header block explaining that two labels were treated as potentially equivalent, pending confirmation, protects the record if someone later reads only the rows. The aim is a sheet that a colleague can pick up cold and understand without asking you what you meant.

The same habit is helpful when you compare public semiconductor materials or silicon recovery catalogues. Copy the category heading as printed and record any uncertainty in the comparison sheet before you ask the supplier.

Keeping the sheet about records, not specifications

It is tempting, once two versions are side by side, to start comparing technical detail. Resist that for this worksheet. The comparison sheet is a purchasing record: it captures what each public version said, when it was shown, when it was retrieved, and who is following up. It is not a specification, a compliance check or a price record.

Leave composition, operating parameters, processing details, legal or regulatory status, prices and any real commitments out of the sheet. Those belong in formal documents exchanged with the supplier, not in a reconciliation worksheet built from public pages. If a colleague asks you to add a technical comparison, point them to the appropriate channel rather than expanding this sheet.

A short review routine before you file the sheet

Before the sheet goes into the sourcing file, run a quick review. These timings are author heuristics, not research findings, and you should adjust them to your own workload.

First, check that every row has all six fields filled, with "none shown" used where a date is absent rather than a blank cell. Allow a few minutes for this pass.

Second, confirm that the two source URLs are recorded exactly and that both retrieval dates are present in the header block. A minute or two is usually enough.

Third, read the open questions as if you were a colleague seeing them for the first time. Each should name a specific uncertainty and have an owner. Rewrite any question that could be read two ways.

Fourth, check that no technical, pricing or compliance content has crept into the sheet. If it has, move it to the correct document and note where it went.

Finally, add a one-line summary at the top stating which two versions were compared and what remains open. That line is what most readers will use, so make it accurate rather than reassuring.

When the reconciliation concerns materials or power-module topics, the San Techno products page is a sensible starting point for the public descriptions you may be recording, and the contact page is the right route for follow-up questions rather than the worksheet itself.

When to escalate rather than reconcile

Some differences should not be resolved inside a comparison sheet at all. If two public versions appear to make conflicting statements about a product's suitability for a particular use, or if a change looks material to a purchasing decision, escalate it through the supplier's proper contact route and record the escalation in the sheet.

Escalation is not a failure of the reconciliation process. It is the correct outcome when the public record is ambiguous and the decision matters. The sheet's job is to make that ambiguity visible and to show who is handling it, so that the sourcing file reflects what is known, what is uncertain, and what has been asked.
